i. Today’s reception is being sponsored by the College of Pharmacy - Thank you Dean LaPlante!
ii. Call for Nominations: At the October Faculty Senate meeting, Sens. Kendall Moore, William Krieger, and Alison Roberts were chosen as this year’s Nominating Committee. Per Section 5.2 of the Senate By-Laws, the Nominating Committee shall prepare a slate of candidates for one (1) one-year and two (2) two-year vacancies on the Executive Committee. The Executive Committee Election shall be held May 7, 2026. Please reach out to a member of the Nominating Committee if you are interested in this role.

iii. Announcement regarding making rooms available to rent to grad students - VP Preisser offered a reminder about concerns recently shared by the Graduate Student Association related to the temporary closure of Graduate Village. Dozens of students remain on a waitlist for housing. In an effort to ensure that all enrolled students have access to appropriate housing, FSEC encourages faculty and staff, especially those who live in close proximity to campus, to consider offering a room to rent. VP Preisser encouraged faculty to spread the word, and suggested that they explore relevant housing webpages or reach out to him directly for more information.

iv. ‘All-hands’ curriculum meeting prior to the start of fall semester 2026 - VP Preisser announced that the Faculty Senate and Vice Provost Adams are co-hosting a mandatory meeting on September 1, at 1 pm, aimed at improving curriculum proposal quality and review process consistency in Kuali. The meeting would be required for Deans and Associate Deans who have approval roles in the CMS and it is strongly recommended that the faculty chairs of college-level curriculum committees also attend. More information will be forthcoming but affected parties need to make sure this meeting is in their calendars.
2. Disposition of the Minutes - Faculty Senate President Williams
i. Minutes of the Faculty Senate Meeting of 3/12/26 were approved.
3. Activities of the Executive Committee - Senate Vice President Preisser noted the important work of FSEC reflected in the following minutes. There were no questions.
i. Executive Committee Meetings of March 6, March 13, and March 27, 2026 meetings. (No meeting on 3/20 due to Spring Break.)
d. Recommendations of the Faculty Senate Executive Committee: FSEC recommends the following bills:

i. Approval of Faculty Senate Meeting Calendar for AY 2026-2027. Pres. Williams noted that FSEC has recommended a meeting calendar that prioritizes ‘third Thursdays’ for consistency, while avoiding holidays, breaks, and cultural or religious celebrations that preclude work. The calendar was approved.
ii. Bill 2025-2026-FSEC-09: Amendments to UM 5.78.10 - 5.78.12 regarding the Joint Committee on Online and Distance Learning - Continued from the 2/19/26 And 3/12/26 meetings. Pres. Williams noted the proposal had been discussed by the faculty senate at previous meetings and is now offered for approval. It was moved to the senate docket for action by FSEC and was seconded. Questions were raised from the floor about some particulars of the bill and FSEC members responded. Comments were also offered from the floor noting one senator’s outstanding concerns about the bill as written. A motion was made to table the bill in its entirety. Pres. Williams noted a motion to table is not debatable or amendable and requires a ⅔ majority for approval. The motion to table passed.
iii. Ratification of appointment to the Space Allocation Committee: Leon Thiem, representing the College of Engineering. A motion to ratify was approved.

iv. FSEC Bill 2025-2026-12 regarding precluding use of the Veteran’s Day holiday as an instructional day - VP Preisser noted that while State and Federal calendars list Veteran’s Day as a holiday, language in the University Manual does not preclude its use as an instructional day. FSEC sought to clear up any confusion via the proposed amendment, which was moved for action by FSEC and seconded from the floor. College of Education senators inquired whether or not the current proposal was the result of their petition last month to amend the University Manual to preclude the use of Indigenous People’sDay/Columbus (IP/C) Day as an instructional day. VP Preisser answered affirmatively, explaining that the detailed review of UM Sec. 8.70.25 that occurred with their proposal marked the first time the ACC, CBUM and FSEC had all taken an in-depth look at the relevant language in quite some time, and the question of Veteran’s Day seemed to warrant clarification independent of what happens with the IP/C Day legislation, which is still under consideration. In response to further questions, VP Preisser confirmed that approval of the subject bill does not preclude approval of the IP/C Day bill, but he acknowledged that the constrained number of available instructional days in certain fall semesters certainly makes the Calendar Committee’s work more challenging.

5. SPECIAL REPORTS:
1. Bill 2025-2026-Joint-01, a joint proposal of the University Administration, FSEC, and the SCLC regarding reorganization of the Office of the University Ombuds. Faculty Senate President Williams explained that the proposal was the result of work done by multiple committees and individuals over the course of more than a year. Also, the plan to professionalize the Office of the Ombuds had been discussed at previous senate meetings, including, most recently, the March 12 meeting. With no further questions or discussion, there was a motion and second to approve the proposal. The motion was approved.
2. Student Senate Resolution on Accessible Education Material, as approved by the Student Senate on March 25, 2026. Tabled.

3. Kuali pause for proposal submissions, summer 2026 - Faculty Senate Specialist Spitale, FSEC member Trimm, and Enrollment Services Assoc. Director Humphrey. Specialist Spitale explained that a pause in new Kuali submissions is planned for the summer months to allow system administrators the opportunity to make much-needed updates to workflows and user experience features. All proposals entered by 5/15 will still advance through the approval process to the Dean-level of review. Any proposal not approved by the relevant dean by 6/1 will revert to draft form. Such drafts will remain in the system and will still be viewable, but will need to be resubmitted at a later date to advance toward approval. Normal proposal submission procedures and workflows will resume on 8/15. Additional information is available via the Curriculum Toolkit on the Faculty Senate’s webpage. Questions from the floor were offered, including inquiries about the degree to which suggestions from the various college curriculum committees factor into the update. It was noted that the current effort is focused more on compliance with the curricular streamlining initiative approved by the faculty senate earlier this year, but it is hoped that this year’s initiative will lay the groundwork for future short pauses wherein incremental process improvements like those that would be suggested by the curriculum committees might be made.

6. REPORTS OF STANDING AND SPECIAL COMMITTEES
a. Curriculum and Standards Committee - Chair Furong Xu was on hand to field questions about the reports. The following were advanced by the Committee, seconded from the floor, and approved.
i. Bill No. 2025-2026-07A, Courses, covering one new temporary course and fifteen new permanent courses, as well as numerous course modifications across five colleges.
ii. Bill No. 2025-2026-07B, Programs, covering multiple program modifications, including to specializations and minors, in the Colleges of Arts and Sciences, Business, Engineering, Health Sciences, and the College of the Environment and Life Sciences.
iii. Bill No. 2025-2026-07C, covering two new programs, one in the College of Arts and Sciences and one in the College of the Environment and Life Sciences.
b. Curricular Reports from the Graduate Council to the Faculty Senate - The following bills were advanced by the Committee, seconded from the floor, and approved.

i. Bill 2025-2026-06A, Courses, covering multiple course modifications across seven colleges, along with several new courses in the the Colleges of Arts and Sciences, Business, Education, Engineering, Pharmacy, and the College of the Environment and Life Sciences.
ii. Bill 2025-2026-06B, Programs, including several program modifications, along with new certificates and specializations.
c. Centers and Institutes Review Committee - Chair Porto - The CIRC is required to present annually on any new Centers and Institutes and on the rechartering status of other C/I’s reviewed. Tabled to the May 7 meeting.

d. Teaching, Advising, and Admissions Committee Annual Report- Chair Romanow praised her fellow committee members and noted they have had a very busy and productive year. The TAAC was involved in the review and approval of several key pieces of legislation this year, including the creation of a President’s List and modernizing the Second Grade Option. They were also involved in the curricular streamlining initiative and the reconfiguration of the Honors Program. As a result of legislation approved last year, the Committee now has a role to play in Admissions and is still determining, with AVP Libutti’s help, how that new charge will be implemented. In terms of future priorities, the Committee has been tasked with looking at UM provisions related to academic dishonesty, especially where it intersects with grade disputes. The Committee hopes to craft relevant amendments for consideration next year.

e.
Budget and Administration Committee Annual Report - Chair Triki explained that his committee’s primary task this year has been to try to measure faculty sentiment toward the new budget mode via a survey distributed broadly to the community.
As of now, the Committee intends, according to Chair Triki, to share their results with the Financial Strategy and Planning Office so that a conversation about improving messaging might be had.
It has not yet been decided how the data collected might otherwise be shared or disseminated.
Based on the survey results, the Committee had concluded that there seems to be a serious disconnect between the actual outcomes of the budget model roll-out and the faculty’s perception of those outcomes.
As examples, a majority of those surveyed did not see the new model as improving transparency or ensuring a more fair allocation of resources across colleges.
Chair Triki suggested that expanding dissemination of information about the details and mechanics of the budget might result in more positive perceptions.
VP Jenkins asked if current sentiment around higher education generally might have colored the survey results.

She enumerated several recent and ongoing concerns and challenges facing universities around the country (constrained research funding, various Federal actions, outside influence and interference in curricular matters, etc.) and suggested that the current landscape likely has a negative ‘baseline mood’ undercurrent that would be hard to measure.
Chair Triki agreed that the survey probably did roll out at an unfortunate time for measuring faculty understanding and satisfaction.
He noted that one positive takeaway from the results was the degree to which faculty are engaged and paying attention, and he praised their resilience in the face of unrelenting bad news.

f. Committee on Technology and Infrastructure Annual Report - Chair Wallace noted the many projects his committee tackled this year, including providing input to improve Brightspace and EdTech operations, helping to recreate a searchable classroom database, and suggesting strategies for improving the IT contracts/software approval process. They also provided important outreach to faculty about their roles in website editing, and helped raise awareness about current IT Policies. Priorities for next year will include understanding faculty needs and habits around responsible AI use in research, and aiding in Brightspace file recovery and migration, among other things.
7. CALL for NEW BUSINESS - None.
8. ADJOURNMENT - The meeting adjourned at 4:35 pm.

Candidate Statement I would like to boast that my work on committees spanning the curriculum, assessment, general education, academic planning, technologies, and accreditation has given me a keen ability to understand the inner workings and needs of the Faculty Senate and the University itself.
In reality, I simply enjoy working with bright, caring people across the University to ﬁnd creative, meaningful, sometimes elegant and often astoundingly effective solutions to problems facing this institution.
The connections we have between colleges, disciplines, and administrative units are both our strength and our guide.
They remind us of the importance of taking care of one another, working constructively across academic and institutional boundaries, and protecting shared governance, academic freedom, and advocacy itself during tumultuous times.
URI has weathered past transformational challenges, including the complete reform of the General Education Program, the global pandemic, and the ﬁrst years of the intensifying demographic cliff we are facing.

Uncertainty seems to be the word that best encapsulates the challenges we face today — challenges that affect the process of decision-making itself.
I do not have all the answers, but I have spent a long time learning how to ﬁnd them with others, and I would be honored to do that work on behalf of URI's faculty as a member of the Executive Committee or in any other capacity.

1 University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees Regulations Regarding Use of University Property [DRAFT 20241008 CC] Introduction As noted in the University of Rhode Island’s Mission Statement and consistent with University values, the University of Rhode (also “University” or “URI”) is committed to high- quality education, community engagement, and the freedom to learn, teach, create, and conduct research with integrity in the pursuit and dissemination of new knowledge aimed at contributing to the public good.
The management of University Property and other resources is paramount to meeting that mission.
Authority and Applicability Pursuant to Rhode Island General Laws §§ 16-32-2 and 16 -32-2.1, the University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees is empowered to make rules and regulations for the control and use of Univ ersity Property while the President of the University is responsible for the general management of University Property.

These regulations apply to all users of University Property , including all members of the University community (students, faculty, staff, and affiliates) and third parties (individuals, groups, and members of the public) who wish to use any University Property for any purpose.
Definitions University Operations.
All teaching , research, community engagement, and business functions, as well as any other official activity of the University.
University Property.
Property belonging to the State of Rhode Island and held in trust by the University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees; property held by the University of Rhode Island or any of its component units in its own name; and property owned by third parties but assigned to, occupied by, or managed by the University or any of its component units.
University Property includes all real property, including without limitation land, buildings and other structures, fences, driveways and walkways, and other permanent improvements and associated infrastructure .
For the purposes of these regulations, property leased or licensed to a third party is excluded from the definition of University Property. 1.

General The primary purpose of University Property is to support the University’s mission.
Every individual and group using University Property is expected to use it in a manner that (i) complies with all applicable laws, policies, procedures, rules, and regulations; (ii) is safe and responsible; (iii) maintains and protects the integrity, cleanliness, and functionality of the University Property; (iv) does not materially and substantially disrupt or interfere with University Operations; and (v) does not impinge upon the individual rights of another person or group.

2 Access to and use of University Property is governed by the University, not by colleges, departments, or administrative units.
Individual colleges, departments, and administrative units may adopt guidelines governing the use of University Property allocated for their specific use provided that such guidelines are consistent with these regulations.
Space is allocated pursuant to the University’s policy on Allocation and Utilization of Space. 2.
Limitations and Prohibited Activities The University may establish reasonable standards and limitations regarding the time, place, and manner of use for any University Property, including access to certain areas within a building, entire buildings themselves, or specified areas of University Property, by both the general public and the University community.
The University also has the right to restrict access t o any and all University Property, including the campus(es) as a whole, as necessary to address safety and/or security concerns.

Specific requirements relative to the limitations and prohibited activities (e.g., building hours, decibel levels, posting, etc.) may be developed by the Department of Public Safety and posted on the Public Safety website. a.

It advances student success, retention, timely degree completion, and career readiness.
The program’s applied focus, interdisciplinary design, and integration of experiential learning opportunities support students in developing market- relevant skills that align with workforce needs.
By embedding internships, project-based learning, and applied AI coursework throughout the curriculum, the program enhances students’ engagement, persistence, and post-graduation outcomes while positioning URI graduates to succeed in a rapidly evolving, AI-enabled economy.
The vision is to provide students with deep knowledge of AI systems and expertise in transferring and applying AI to a variety of problem types.

This program will cover knowledge of the AI ecosystem including the ability to work in interdisciplinary teams with data and domain experts to collect, clean organize, and sample data, match the problem and data to the right intelligent computational tool (there are many types of AI, each with its strengths and weaknesses), tailor, build on top of, and adapt these tools to the problems at hand, support the safe, secure, ethical and accurate reporting of the results to domain experts, and guide teams in deciding if the analytical results make sense.
Students will learn how to use, tailor and augment AI so that the AI can serve as assistants in problem solving, with the human as the master, well versed in the interpretation, and ethical and societal implications of the use of the powerful AI that they will wield.
All of this is in the context of a world in which educators and potential employers are concerned with the lack of digital skills among today’s students and graduates.
To be well educated and prepared for the modern workplace, students must learn to acquire applied technology skills and also to transfer these technologies to specific problems as they arise.

Thus this program is not intended to train students to develop new AI, but to become experts in mastering, adapting, building upon, and deploying existing and evolving intelligent computational artifacts.
We will help students to master the AI tools of today but also help them to understand that these are only contemporary examples to sharpen their problem solving, and learning skills, and give them a leg up as they enter the workplace.
As the world changes and embraces new technologies such as digital twins, and quantum computing, both already inextricably intertwined with AI, we propose a major that is flexible enough that it can evolve with emerging intelligent technologies.
The program advances the University’s goals by preparing students to address complex real-world challenges through the responsible and creative application of emerging technologies.
The curriculum integrates applied coursework, project-based learning, writing-intensive experiences, and internships, ensuring that students develop both technical expertise and transferable skills that support career readiness and lifelong learning.

The program reflects the University’s commitment to interdisciplinary problem-solving and collaboration across colleges and departments.
The program embeds ethical reasoning, equity, and societal impact throughout the curriculum, aligning with the University’s emphasis on responsible scholarship, civic engagement, and public good.
The program also contributes to the University’s role in supporting economic development, innovation, and the future of work in Rhode Island and beyond.

The Applied AI M ajor is justified by a fundamental shift in how artificial intelligence is developed and used in practice.
Innovation in AI is no longer driven primarily by building algorithms from scratch; instead, it increasingly relies on the creative and programmatic use of existing models, platforms, and tools to design new products, services, and decision systems.
M odern workplaces expect graduates who can integrate pretrained models, APIs, and data pipelines into real- world applications,d combining technical fluency with domain knowledge to solve practical problems.
This requires more than traditional computer or data science or statistics training: it demands an applied understanding of how to select appropriate models, adapt them to specific contexts, validate their outputs, and embed them into larger systems responsibly.
An Applied AI M ajor addresses this need by preparing students to work at the intersection of data, models, and applications.
Students learn how to manipulate and orchestrate existing AI tools programmatically, that is, fine-tuning models, designing prompts and workflows, building intelligent pipelines, and translating outputs into usable products.

Equally important, they learn how to evaluate model limitations, detect bias, protect privacy, and communicate results clearly to nontechnical stakeholders.
This combination of technical practice and critical judgment reflects how AI is actually deployed in industry, government, and research labs.
Research on Human–AI teaming [Vanshika Vats, et al. (2024)] shows that integrating large pretrained models with human decision making enhances applied problem solving and decision quality across domains underscoring the importance of skills to programmatically manipulate and integrate existing AI models.
By focusing on the intelligent use of existing AI models rather than solely on algorithm development, the major equips students with transferable competencies: problem formulation, tool selection, system integration, and ethical reasoning.
These skills enable graduates not only to build AI- driven products today, but also to adapt quickly as new “d” technologies emerge.
The Applied AI M ajor therefore fills a distinct and timely educational need, preparing students to have practical knowledge of AI, and to be creators and integrators of intelligent systems rather than passive users of them.

Student Demand.

Demand is expected to come from multiple sources, including current URI students seeking applied, career-relevant skills, working professionals looking to upskill or reskill, and students drawn to interdisciplinary programs that connect business, technology, and societal impact.
Informal indicators such as student interest in related courses and certificates, growing enrollment in adjacent programs, and employer demand for applied analytical and digital skills suggest a steady but manageable level of initial interest.
Projections assume gradual growth as the program gains visibility and establishes a track record.
Regional Competition.
Regionally, there are relatively few programs that combine applied, workforce-oriented content with strong experiential and interdisciplinary elements.
While competing institutions may offer related degrees or certificates, many are either more narrowly technical, less applied, or structured primarily for full-time students.

The program’s design differentiates it through its applied focus, integration with existing strengths at the University, and alignment with regional workforce needs, supporting realistic enrollment assumptions without relying on displacement from peer institutions.
Capacity-Based Assumptions.
Enrollment projections are intentionally aligned with existing instructional and advising capacity in the early years.
Growth assumptions are modest and phased, with increases tied to demonstrated demand and the planned addition of advising support and faculty resources in later stages.
This approach ensures that financial projections are grounded in operational feasibility rather than aspirational targets.
Overall, the enrollment figures used in the financial projections reflect a balanced assessment of student interest, regional competition, and institutional capacity, supporting a financially responsible and sustainable program launch.
